title: Folio 3: The Blind King Who Ruled Twice
description: A Sultan who reigned for five months is locked in a fortress by his own brother, and the world forgets him. Ten years later, a mutinous army drags him out and crowns him again. This is the strange fate of Amir Muhammad, son of Mahmud of Ghazni, and of the brother who took his throne.
source: Tarikh-e Beyhaqi (Muhammad in the fortress after Tiginabad, 421 AH / 1030 CE; Masud's departure for India after Dandanqan, 431-432 AH / 1040 CE), with the later chroniclers for the mutiny at Marikala, Masud's death at Giri and Mawdud's victory near Nangarhar (432 AH / 1041 CE)
cold_open: A mountain pass near the Indus, in the winter of the year one thousand and forty. A blind man is led out among a crowd of soldiers. Ten years ago, he was a king. Tonight, they want him to be king again.

extra_shorts.hook: A blind prisoner is told he is king again

extra_shorts.from: Now, at this point, I want to pause
extra_shorts.hook: The Persian line that warns every king

paragraphs: Welcome to The Honest Historian. I'm Mehdi Rahmani, and this is Folio Three. Last week, a young Sultan woke up in his camp to find that his army had gone over to his brother. By evening, he was a prisoner in a fortress.
Today, I want to climb up to that fortress and ask a simple question. What happened to him? Because the answer is one of the strangest turns of fortune in the whole history of the Ghaznavids.

Let me remind you who he was. His name was Muhammad, the younger son of Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni. Mahmud ruled a vast empire from his capital, Ghazni, in the mountains of what is now Afghanistan. Before he died in the year one thousand and thirty, he chose Muhammad as his heir, not his elder son Masud.

So for about five months, Muhammad was Sultan. Then the generals changed sides, and Masud took the throne. Muhammad was taken to a fortress near Tiginabad, in the dry south of Afghanistan, with his family and his servants, and put under guard.

Beyhaqi gives us a few precious glimpses of him there. For two or three days, he sat in silence, lost in sorrow. When a letter came from his brother, telling him he would stay in the fortress, honorably, but under guard, he grew troubled. And an old official told him gently that what was meant to be, had been.
That was where we left him. A young man in his early thirties, the son of the most famous king of his age, sitting behind stone walls, while the world went on without him.
What happened next is not easy to tell, and I want to be honest with you about why.

The History of Beyhaqi was once enormous. It filled some thirty volumes. Only a part of it survives, the part that covers the reign of Masud. Beyhaqi does not stop his story to follow a prisoner from year to year. So for much of Muhammad's life after this, we have only scattered lines, in Beyhaqi and in other chroniclers.

Here is what most of them agree on. Muhammad was blinded. In that world, blinding was a cruel but common way of making a prince harmless. A blind man, by custom, could not rule. When exactly it was done, and on whose order, the sources do not fully agree, and some modern scholars have their doubts about the early date. But by the end of our story, every account calls him the blind Muhammad.
And so, for about ten years, he lived as a prisoner. His sons grew up in captivity with him. Outside, his brother ruled the empire.
Now let's step outside the fortress and look at those ten years.

They did not go well for Masud. He was brave and generous, but he was also stubborn, and he often refused good advice. In the north and west of his empire, a new power was rising. These were the Seljuqs, Turkish nomads from the steppes, who moved with their herds and their horsemen into the lands of Khorasan.

At first, they seemed like a nuisance. Then they became a danger. And in the year one thousand and forty, at a place called Dandanqan, in the desert near the city of Merv, Masud's great army met them in battle and was broken. We will tell that story properly in a later folio. For now, all you need to know is this: after Dandanqan, the western half of the empire was lost.

Masud went back to Ghazni. He was shaken, and he did not trust the men around him. And he decided to do something that alarmed his whole court. He would leave Ghazni and go to India, to the lands his family held across the Indus River, to gather new strength there.

His ministers begged him to stay. Beyhaqi, who was in the royal chancery at the time, lets us feel how uneasy the court was. But Masud would not listen. He loaded up his treasury, his family and his household, and set off toward India.
And here is the detail that changes everything.

Masud did not leave his blind brother behind. According to the later chroniclers, he took Muhammad with him on the journey, together with Muhammad's sons. Perhaps he was afraid that if Muhammad stayed in a fortress near Ghazni, someone might use him as the banner for a rebellion.
If that was his fear, he took the danger with him.

The great caravan moved slowly through the mountain passes, heavy with gold. At a pass called Marikala, near the Indus, discipline collapsed. The soldiers and the palace slaves began to plunder the treasure. And once they had done that, they knew there was no going back. Masud would never forgive them. So they needed a new king.
They went to Muhammad.
Think about that moment. A blind man, who has spent about ten years as a prisoner, is told by a crowd of soldiers that he is Sultan again.

It is said that he did not want it. Some of the accounts suggest that he had to be pressed, even threatened, before he agreed. Whether that was true reluctance, or simply wisdom, we cannot know. A blind king at the head of a mutinous army was not a king for long in that world, and he may have known it.
But he accepted. And because he could not see to govern, the real power went to his son Ahmad, a young man with his own anger and his own ambitions.

Masud, the Sultan who had once taken the throne from his brother without a battle, now lost it to his brother in the same way. He was seized and sent as a prisoner to a fortress called Giri, in what is now the north-west of Pakistan. And there, early in the year one thousand and forty one, he was killed. The chroniclers point mainly at Ahmad, Muhammad's son, as the one who ordered it. Some say the order came in Muhammad's name.
Two brothers. Two fortresses. Ten years apart.

Now, at this point, I want to pause and tell you something about Beyhaqi. Again and again in his book, he warns his readers about this world, and how quickly it turns. In one famous passage, he writes a line that every student of Persian prose knows. Let me say it in Persian, and then in English.
Ahmaq marda ke del dar in jahan bandad, ke nemati bedahad va zesht baz setanad.
Foolish is the man who binds his heart to this world, for it gives a blessing, and then takes it back in an ugly way.
Beyhaqi wrote that about another man, on another day. But I cannot think of a better line for the two sons of Sultan Mahmud.
The story is not quite over. Masud had sons too. One of them, Mawdud, was in the north, in the region of Balkh, when the news reached him. He gathered an army and marched south to avenge his father.

In the spring of the year one thousand and forty one, Mawdud met the army of Muhammad and Ahmad near Nangarhar, in the east of today's Afghanistan, not far from the modern city of Jalalabad. Muhammad's side was defeated. And this time, there was no fortress and no second chance. Muhammad was put to death, and so were his sons, Ahmad among them. On the field of his victory, it is said, Mawdud founded a town and called it Fathabad, the town of victory.
So the blind king's second reign lasted only a few months. Like his first.
What is the point of this sad story? Why does Beyhaqi's world remember it?

I think it is because it shows us something that the great chronicles of kings often hide. A throne is not a safe place. It does not belong to the man who sits on it. It belongs, for a moment, to whoever can hold it, and the next moment it is gone. Muhammad was crowned, imprisoned, blinded, crowned again, and killed. Masud was the winner of Folio Two and the victim of Folio Three. Neither of them, in the end, was the master of his own fate.

Beyhaqi did not watch these events from far away. He was a secretary at Masud's court. He knew these men. And he chose, again and again, to write about the cost of power as well as its glory. That is the honesty that makes him worth reading a thousand years later.
If there is one lesson here, it is this: be careful whom you lock away, because fortune keeps the key.

Next week, we step back two centuries, to the court of the caliphs in Baghdad. Beyhaqi tells a story there about a proud general named Afshin, a nobleman named Bu Dulaf, and a judge who risked everything to save a life. It is one of the most gripping scenes in his whole book.

If you enjoyed this story, follow the show so you don't miss the next one, and share it with someone who loves history. I'm Mehdi Rahmani. This episode was retold from the Persian original of the History of Beyhaqi, and narrated with an AI rendering of my own voice. Thank you for listening.
